questions.enonce_markdown: a) Identify and explain the philosophical problem raised in the situation above. (4 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**The problem: the foundation of morality, or "Why be moral?" (the relation between justice, self-interest and power).**

The story of the ring of Gyges is told in the *Republic* to challenge Socrates' defence of justice. It asks: **if a person could do whatever he wished without being seen, caught or punished, would he still have any reason to be just?** If the answer is no, then people are just only because of **fear** of detection, punishment or loss of reputation, and justice is a burden accepted for its consequences. If the answer is yes, then justice has a value **in itself**, independent of its rewards.

The problem concerns the **motive** of moral action (inner conviction or external sanction), the nature of man (naturally selfish or capable of virtue), and the effect of **impunity and unchecked power** on conduct.

questions.enonce_markdown: (b) Reformulate the problem in a) above into a solvable unit. (3 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
> **Is justice (morality) chosen only out of fear of being discovered and punished, or would a rational person still choose to act justly if he could act unjustly with complete impunity?**

Sub-questions that make it solvable: Is it true that all men naturally seek their own advantage? Is the unjust person who is never discovered really better off and happier than the just person? What is the value of justice apart from its consequences?

questions.enonce_markdown: (c) On what grounds can the position above be justified? (7 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
The position is that **a person with the ring is free to do all he wishes, and would do so**: morality is only a constraint imposed by fear of being seen, and falls away when impunity is certain. It can be justified as follows.

1. **Egoism as the law of human nature.** In the story as told in the *Republic*, the claim is that every man naturally pursues his own advantage (the desire to have more than his share) and is turned aside by law and custom only by force. *Hobbes* similarly holds that men seek their own preservation and gain, and keep agreements only because of the sword of the sovereign.
2. **Justice as a convention born of fear.** The account given in the *Republic* is that justice is a **compromise**: the best condition would be to do wrong without being punished, the worst to suffer wrong without being able to defend oneself; men agree to laws because they cannot get the best and fear the worst. On the social contract view, laws and morals exist for mutual protection, and where the sanction disappears, so does the reason to obey.
3. **Justice as the interest of the stronger.** *Thrasymachus*, in the *Republic*, holds that justice is whatever serves the stronger party; whoever has absolute power need not be just.
4. **The social role of reputation.** People often behave well because they are observed: the appearance of justice brings honour, trust and reward. If one could keep the reward of appearing just while doing wrong unseen, the rational choice would be to do wrong.
5. **Experience.** Power and anonymity do tend to corrupt: officials who are not controlled, people who act anonymously on the internet, and persons in a crowd behave worse than when they are identified.

These grounds make the position plausible: they explain why laws, police, courts and public opinion are needed.

questions.enonce_markdown: (d) Is the justification above tenable? (6 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
The justification is **not tenable as a complete account of morality**, although it contains a partial truth.

1. **Plato's reply.** *Socrates* answers that justice is the **health and harmony of the soul**, in which reason rules the appetites. The unjust man, even unseen and powerful, is the **slave of his desires** and has a disordered soul; he cannot be happy. Injustice harms the doer first. Happiness is not the satisfaction of every wish.
2. **Kant.** The moral worth of an act lies in its being done **from duty**, not from fear or interest. The categorical imperative asks whether the maxim can be universalised: if everyone used a ring of invisibility to take what he wanted, property, trust and society would collapse, so the maxim contradicts itself. Morality does not depend on whether anyone is watching.
3. **Aristotle.** Virtue is a settled disposition acquired by habit; the virtuous person acts well **also when unobserved**, because he finds the noble action itself worthwhile. Man is by nature a social being who flourishes only in community, so that betraying others also destroys the conditions of his own happiness (friendship, trust).
4. **Experience.** Many people act justly without being seen (they return a lost wallet, give anonymously, refuse a bribe), and **conscience** punishes wrongdoing from within. The position confuses what many people **do** under impunity with what they **ought** to do, and ignores the case of those who are good.
5. **Hidden premise.** The argument assumes that the unjust man is happy provided he is not discovered. This is exactly what is in question.

**Its partial truth.** Anonymity and unchecked power do tempt people to wrong, which shows that **institutions, laws and accountability** are necessary and not only good will. A balanced view is that morality needs both **inner conviction** (conscience, virtue) and **external control** (law and oversight).

questions.enonce_markdown: (e) How relevant is the problem at stake to our society today? (5 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
The problem is **very relevant** to our society.

- **Corruption and impunity.** In public life, officials who manage funds with little oversight are in the position of the bearer of the ring: embezzlement, bribery and abuse of power flourish where the chance of being caught is low. This shows why **transparency, audits, an independent judiciary and a free press** are needed.
- **Anonymity in the digital age.** Social networks and the internet give a kind of invisibility: hate messages, fraud and cyber-crime are easier when the author cannot be identified.
- **School and daily life.** Cheating in examinations, tax evasion and traffic offences are tempting when no one is watching; moral education should aim at conscience and not only at fear of punishment.
- **African communal ethics.** In many African societies a person's conduct is judged by the community, and the ancestors are believed to watch over the living; in the ethic of *ubuntu* a person is a person through other persons, so that harming others is harming oneself. The ring of Gyges invites us to compare this communal view with that of Western individualism.
- **Leadership and whistle-blowing.** The problem reminds us to protect those who report wrongdoing and to ask what kind of person we become when we hold power.
